builder_plan.scenario: Your coding assistant makes changes that still need substantial repair before merging.
builder_plan.change: Try the technique on held-out issues from a repository with reliable tests.
builder_plan.baseline: The same coding agent, repository snapshot, tools, and token budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct patches, regression failures, human repair time, and total cost per accepted change.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: FlowPlan: Reducing the Token Cost of Coding Agents with Abstraction-Guided Planning and Verification
summary: FlowPlan replaces the coding agent's iterative loop of re-reading raw source and re-running tests after each edit with localization, explicit repair planning as graph deltas on per-function control-flow or data-flow graphs, and a structural comparison of planned versus observed changes followed by a final verification. The cost is the engineering required to build and maintain per-language graph extraction and delta-comparison tooling plus extra planning steps, which adds complexity and may add latency per repair even as total tokens fall. It can fail where the abstraction mislocalizes the fault, where the planned graph delta does not capture the needed semantic change, or where gains shrink with stronger models, as the Sonnet 5 results (0.72-0.94x) show much smaller savings than Haiku.
rationale: The token-cost reduction is substantial and preserves resolution rate, making it attractive for API-budget-constrained teams running coding agents, but it requires implementing language-specific program-abstraction tooling and the savings vary sharply by model and benchmark, so it warrants a pilot on the reader's own repositories before production adoption.
technique: Abstraction-guided planning and verification for coding agents

claims.statement: FlowPlan replaces the coding agent's iterative loop of re-reading raw source and re-running tests after each edit with localization, explicit repair planning as graph deltas on per-function control-flow or data-flow graphs, and a structural comparison of planned versus observed changes followed by a final verification. The cost is the engineering required to build and maintain per-language graph extraction and delta-comparison tooling plus extra planning steps, which adds complexity and may add latency per repair even as total tokens fall. It can fail where the abstraction mislocalizes the fault, where the planned graph delta does not capture the needed semantic change, or where gains shrink with stronger models, as the Sonnet 5 results (0.72-0.94x) show much smaller savings than Haiku.

With Claude Haiku 4.5, FlowPlan uses 0.32-0.35x baseline tokens on SWE-bench Verified (roughly a 3x reduction) and 0.46-0.47x on SWE-bench Pro, with no significant change in resolution rate across all six benchmark-model settings; token savings are significant in five of six settings.
